q.q: After trauma, a permanent incisor sits out of occlusion (shorter than its neighbours). Which injury is this?
q.e: An intruded tooth is driven into the alveolar bone, so its incisal edge sits short of the occlusal plane. It is usually immobile with a high metallic percussion note. An extruded tooth looks longer and hits first, and a laterally luxated tooth is usually locked in a displaced position with an occlusal interference.
q.c: Consistent with a related Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 question (S01-Q48-A)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S01-Q48-A cites: Sigurdsson A, et al. Recommended Guidelines of the American Association of Endodontists for the Treatment of Traumatic Dental Injuries. J Endod. 2026;52(8):1237-1253. doi:10.1016/j.joen.2026.04.002.
q.n: The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.q: When is a mandibular lingual bar major connector contraindicated?
o: Healthy periodontal support on all abutments
Shallow lingual vestibule (less than about 8 mm from the gingival margins to the floor of the mouth)
A Kennedy Class I edentulous arch
q.e: A lingual bar needs about 8 mm of vertical space: roughly 4 mm for the bar plus 3–4 mm of clearance below the gingival margins. With a shallow floor of mouth there is no room, so a lingual plate is used instead.
q.c: Consistent with a related Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 question (S06-Q167)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S06-Q167 cites: Carr AB et al. McCracken's Removable Partial Prosthodontics. Lingual plate indications.
q.n: The recall gave the two vestibule options; the other two were written in. The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.q: Which orthodontic bracket and archwire would be most suitable for a patient with a jewellery (nickel) allergy?
o: Nickel steel bracket with stainless steel wire
Stainless steel bracket with aluminum wire
Ceramic bracket with stainless steel wire
q.e: Jewellery allergy is almost always nickel allergy. Ceramic brackets contain no nickel, and stainless steel contains about 8–12% nickel, so the best choice pairs a ceramic bracket with a non-stainless wire. Nickel-free titanium (TMA/beta-titanium) wires are the usual choice in practice.
q.c: Answer worked out by reasoning; Not covered in Rafi' Al-Maqam 16. ⚠ Check the wire option.
q.r: Where to read more: Proffit WR et al. Contemporary Orthodontics. Orthodontic materials and nickel hypersensitivity.
q.n: As recalled, the wire was "aluminum". There is no aluminium archwire in practice, so the exam option was most likely a nickel-free titanium wire. The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.q: A patient taking clindamycin develops severe diarrhoea. Which organism is responsible?
q.e: Clindamycin is one of the antibiotics most strongly linked to C. difficile overgrowth and pseudomembranous colitis. Stop the drug and refer.
q.c: Confirmed: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 gives the same answer (S10-Q55)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S10-Q55 cites: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. C. diff: Facts for Clinicians. 2026.

q.q: Long scenario: a patient has bleeding, multiple deep periodontal pockets and bone loss. Which bacterium is most associated?
q.e: T. forsythia belongs to the red complex (with P. gingivalis and T. denticola), which is linked to bleeding on probing, deep pockets and attachment loss in periodontitis. S. mutans and lactobacilli are caries organisms, and Actinomyces is an early plaque coloniser.
q.c: Consistent with a related Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 question (S03-Q40-C)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S03-Q40-C cites: Newman MG, Takei HH, Klokkevold PR, Carranza FA, eds. Carranza's Clinical Periodontology. 13th ed. Periodontal microbial complexes.

q.q: A patient taking lisinopril needs a gingival retraction cord. Which agent should be avoided?
q.e: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor, so the patient is hypertensive. Epinephrine-impregnated cord is absorbed through the sulcus and can raise heart rate and blood pressure. Aluminium chloride or ferric sulfate are the safer haemostatic agents.
q.c: Consistent with a related Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 question (S10-Q48)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S10-Q48 cites: Rosenstiel SF et al. Contemporary Fixed Prosthodontics. 6th ed. Gingival displacement; Little and Falace's Dental Management of the Medically Compromised Patient. 10th ed.
q.n: The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.q: Which burs or instruments are used to finish and polish a Class IV composite restoration?
q.c: No answer recorded in the recall
q.r: Where to read more: Ritter AV et al. Sturdevant's Art and Science of Operative Dentistry. Finishing and polishing composite restorations.
q.n: Deema remembered an option of "2 carbide burs and 1 diamond" but not the answer. In general, a Class IV composite is contoured with fine or extra-fine finishing diamonds or 12–30-fluted carbide finishing burs, then polished with graded discs, rubber points and polishing paste.

q.q: A labially positioned tooth has a thin band of keratinized gingiva and is planned for periodontal (mucogingival) surgery. What should be considered first?
o: Orthodontic treatment to move the tooth back into the alveolar bone
q.e: Labial malposition thins the bone and gingiva over the root. Moving the tooth into the alveolar housing first often thickens the tissue and reduces the need for grafting, or improves the result if surgery is still needed.
q.c: Answer worked out by reasoning; Not covered in Rafi' Al-Maqam 16
q.r: Where to read more: Newman MG et al. Newman and Carranza's Clinical Periodontology. Mucogingival therapy and orthodontic considerations.
q.n: The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.q: An irregular brown macule on the palate is an incidental finding. What is the diagnosis?
o: Nevus (the first word was not recalled)
q.c: No answer recorded in the recall
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S10-Q96-D cites: Neville BW, Damm DD, Allen CM, Chi AC. Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology. 5th ed. Oral melanoma.
q.n: Deema couldn't recall the answer. The palate is the most common oral site for a nevus, while melanotic macules are more typical of the lower lip and gingiva. Either way, an irregular pigmented palatal lesion needs a biopsy to rule out melanoma, since the palate is also the most common site of oral melanoma.

q.q: In a complete denture, the "F" sound comes out like "V". Where are the maxillary anterior teeth positioned?
o: Too far anterior and too incisal
Too far anterior and too cervical
q.c: No answer recorded in the recall
q.r: Where to read more: Zarb GA et al. Prosthodontic Treatment for Edentulous Patients. Phonetics and anterior tooth arrangement.
q.n: Deema couldn't recall the answer. For F and V, the incisal edges of the maxillary incisors should lightly touch the wet-dry line of the lower lip. When these sounds are distorted, the incisors are set either too short or long, or too far labial or palatal. Check this one against Zarb (phonetics in complete-denture tooth arrangement).

q.q: Which root of the maxillary first molar is most commonly resected?
q.e: The distobuccal root is the shortest and smallest, sits close to the furcation and is often the one with bone loss. Removing it affects the tooth's support least, so it is the root most often resected.
q.c: Answer worked out by reasoning; Not covered in Rafi' Al-Maqam 16. Saud's File gives the same answer.
q.r: Where to read more: Newman MG et al. Newman and Carranza's Clinical Periodontology. Furcation involvement and root resection.
q.n: The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.q: A patient is a mouth breather. Which appliance is used?
q.c: No answer recorded in the recall
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S07-Q11-H cites: Proffit WR, Fields HW, Larson B, Sarver DM. Contemporary Orthodontics. 7th ed. Respiratory pattern and dentofacial development.
q.n: The recall only said "mouth breather, which appliance"; the options were written in. An oral (vestibular) screen is the habit-breaking appliance that trains lip seal and nasal breathing once any airway obstruction is ruled out. Rapid maxillary expansion is used when there is also a narrow maxilla or crossbite, and Rafi' Al-Maqam 19 gives "expansion" for this topic.

q.q: What is the maximum epinephrine dose per appointment for a patient with significant cardiovascular disease?
q.e: For cardiac patients the limit is 0.04 mg, about two 1.8-mL cartridges of 1:100,000 epinephrine. For a healthy adult the maximum is 0.2 mg.
q.c: Consistent with the October 2026 bank (OCT-65); Not covered in Rafi' Al-Maqam 16
q.r: Where to read more: Malamed SF. Handbook of Local Anesthesia. Vasoconstrictor doses in cardiovascular disease.
q.n: The recall gave 0.04 and 0.01; the other options were written in. The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.q: Long scenario: a patient has brief, unilateral, electric-shock-like facial pain. What is the diagnosis?
q.e: Paroxysms of unilateral electric-shock pain lasting seconds, often set off by light touch at a trigger zone and followed by a refractory period, are classic trigeminal neuralgia.
q.c: Confirmed: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 gives the same answer (S10-Q26)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S10-Q26 cites: International Headache Society. International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd ed. Trigeminal neuralgia criteria.

q.q: Which occlusal scheme is used for a complete denture opposing a removable partial denture?
q.e: A complete denture needs contacts on both sides during excursions to stay stable, so bilateral balanced occlusion is used. Canine guidance and mutually protected occlusion tip a complete denture.
q.c: Consistent with a related Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 question (S06-Q33-A)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S06-Q33-A cites: Zarb GA, Hobkirk J, Eckert S, Jacob R. Prosthodontic Treatment for Edentulous Patients. 13th ed. Complete-denture occlusion.
q.n: The recall gave unilateral and bilateral occlusion; the other options were written in. The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.q: A patient with liver cirrhosis needs local anaesthesia. Which agent should be given?
q.c: No answer recorded in the recall
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S10-Q33-E cites: Little JW, Miller CS, Rhodus NL. Dental Management of the Medically Compromised Patient. 9th ed. Liver disease.
q.n: Deema couldn't recall the answer, and the references disagree. Amides (lidocaine, bupivacaine, prilocaine) are broken down in the liver. Some answer keys therefore pick an ester (procaine). Others pick prilocaine, which is partly metabolised outside the liver, or articaine if it's offered. Whatever the agent, use the lowest dose and check INR and platelets first.

q.q: Histology shows Reed-Sternberg cells. What is the diagnosis?
q.e: Reed-Sternberg cells (large binucleate "owl-eye" cells) are the hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma, which typically presents as painless cervical lymphadenopathy.
q.c: Recall answer; Not covered in Rafi' Al-Maqam 16. Saud's File gives the same answer.
q.r: Where to read more: Neville BW et al. Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology. Hodgkin lymphoma.

q.q: Apertognathia (skeletal open bite) is most commonly associated with which skeletal pattern?
o: Class II division 2 with deep bite
Mandibular retrognathia with a low angle
q.e: Apertognathia is an open bite. Skeletal open bites typically come with excess vertical growth of the posterior maxilla, a long lower face and a steep mandibular plane.
q.c: Recall answer; Salem's Prep gives the same answer (SAL-763). Rafi' Al-Maqam 19 links it to mandibular prognathism instead.
q.r: Where to read more: Proffit WR et al. Contemporary Orthodontics. Vertical problems and long-face pattern.
q.n: The recall gave only "Apertognathia? Maxillary excess"; the question and other options were written around that answer.

q.q: Teeth 18, 17 and 16 are missing, 24 and 26 are missing, and 25 is non-restorable. What is the Kennedy classification?
q.e: Classify after planned extractions, so 25 counts as missing. The right side is a distal-extension space (18, 17, 16), giving Class II. The left side (24–26) is one additional bounded space, so it is modification 1. This assumes 27 is present.
q.c: Applegate's rules as applied in Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 (S06-Q125)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S06-Q125 cites: Carr AB et al. McCracken's Removable Partial Prosthodontics. Applegate rules for Kennedy classification.
q.n: No options were recalled; they were written in. The answer assumes 27 is still present.

q.q: A 14-year-old with Class I malocclusion has a single anterior tooth in crossbite. What is the treatment?
q.e: A single dental anterior crossbite with adequate space in a cooperative patient is corrected with a removable appliance and a Z-spring or finger spring, with posterior bite blocks to open the bite.
q.c: Consistent with a related Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 question (S07-Q29)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S07-Q29 cites: American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry. Management of the Developing Dentition and Occlusion. Reference Manual of Pediatric Dentistry. 2025:497-515.
q.n: The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.q: What is the first tissue reaction 24–48 hours after placing orthodontic force?
q.e: With typical orthodontic forces, blood flow in the compressed PDL is cut off within minutes and the area becomes cell-free (hyalinized) within hours to days. Tooth movement then waits for undermining resorption from the adjacent marrow spaces.
q.c: Answer worked out by reasoning; Not covered in Rafi' Al-Maqam 16. Saud's File gives the same answer.
q.r: Where to read more: Proffit WR et al. Contemporary Orthodontics. The biologic basis of orthodontic therapy.
q.n: The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.q: A radiograph shows loss of the lamina dura and a fibrous-dysplasia-like (ground-glass) bone pattern. Which condition is most likely?
q.e: Hyperparathyroidism causes generalized loss of lamina dura with a granular or ground-glass bone pattern, and sometimes brown tumours.
q.c: Consistent with a related Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 question (S10-Q288-E)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S10-Q288-E cites: White SC, Pharoah MJ. Oral Radiology: Principles and Interpretation. 8th ed. Metabolic bone disease.
q.n: The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.q: A patient has desquamative gingivitis and white striae on the buccal mucosa. What is the diagnosis?
q.e: Desquamative gingivitis has several causes, but bilateral reticular white (Wickham) striae on the buccal mucosa point to lichen planus. Pemphigoid and pemphigus do not produce striae.
q.c: Confirmed: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 gives the same answer (S10-Q52)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S10-Q52 cites: Neville BW et al. Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology. 5th ed. Oral lichen planus and desquamative gingivitis.

q.q: A patient develops an ulcer in the area of 35 and 36 two days after scaling. What is the management?
q.e: A small ulcer after instrumentation is a traumatic ulcer and heals on its own within 1–2 weeks. Review it, and biopsy only if it hasn't healed by about 2 weeks.

q.q: A patient reports a sulfur allergy. Which elastomeric impression material should be avoided?
q.e: Polysulfide (mercaptan rubber) is based on a sulfur-containing polymer. Addition silicone and polyether are sulfur-free alternatives.
q.c: Answer worked out by reasoning; Not covered in Rafi' Al-Maqam 16

q.q: After an episode of erythema multiforme treated with corticosteroids, the patient wants definitive treatment to prevent recurrence. What is given?
q.e: Most recurrent erythema multiforme is triggered by herpes simplex, so continuous antiviral suppression reduces recurrences. Corticosteroids treat the acute episode but don't prevent the next one.
q.c: Confirmed: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 gives the same answer (S10-Q181)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S10-Q181 cites: Glick M, ed. Burket's Oral Medicine. 13th ed. Erythema multiforme; British Association of Dermatologists. Erythema multiforme guidance.

q.q: Infection-control case: what is the first and most important measure to prevent cross-infection?
q.e: Hand hygiene is the single most important measure. It comes before gloving and between every patient, and gloves don't replace it.
q.c: Consistent with a related Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 question (S09-Q63)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S09-Q63 cites: World Health Organization. WHO Guidelines on Hand Hygiene in Health Care. Handwashing and handrubbing technique.

q.q: What is the minimum number of clasp assemblies for a Kennedy Class I RPD?
q.e: A Kennedy Class I (bilateral distal extension) RPD needs one direct retainer on each side, next to each extension, so the minimum is 2. A Class II needs 3, and a Class III needs 4 (quadrilateral).
q.c: Answer worked out by reasoning; Not covered in Rafi' Al-Maqam 16. Saud's File gives the same answer.
q.r: Where to read more: Carr AB et al. McCracken's Removable Partial Prosthodontics. Direct retainers and RPD design.
q.n: The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.q: A newborn has small keratin-filled cysts along the midpalatal raphe. What are they?
q.e: Epstein pearls lie along the midpalatal raphe. Bohn nodules are on the buccal and lingual alveolar ridges or the junction of hard and soft palate, and dental lamina cysts are on the alveolar crest. All resolve on their own.
q.c: Recall answer; Not covered in Rafi' Al-Maqam 16. Rafi' Al-Maqam 19 gives the same answer (R19-OM-120).
q.r: Where to read more: Neville BW et al. Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology. Developmental defects: palatal cysts of the newborn.
q.n: The recall said "Midpalatal — Epstein pearl"; the question and other options were written around that.

q.q: After trauma, a tooth has a cervical root fracture with no mobility (the type of trauma wasn't specified). How long is it splinted?
q.c: No answer recorded in the recall
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S01-Q68 cites: Andreasen JO, Andreasen FM, Andersson L, eds. Textbook and Color Atlas of Traumatic Injuries to the Teeth. 5th ed. Chapter 15, root fractures, pp.377-412, and splinting chapter 39, pp.962-971. Dean JA, ed. McDonald and Avery’s Dentistry for the Child and Adolescent. 11th ed. Chapter 28, dental trauma; exact pages require verification.
q.n: The recall didn't say which injury, so the answer depends on it. A root fracture is splinted for 4 weeks, and up to 4 months for a cervical-third fracture. A subluxation is splinted for up to 2 weeks only for comfort, and a concussion needs no splint.

q.q: Bilateral small round radiolucencies are seen between the first molar and premolar regions of the mandible. What are they?
q.e: The mental foramen appears as a round radiolucency near the premolar apices, bilaterally. It moves relative to the root on angled films, and the tooth tests vital.
q.c: Consistent with a related Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 question (S01-Q19-D)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S01-Q19-D cites: White SC, Pharoah MJ. Oral Radiology: Principles and Interpretation. Periapical anatomy and localization; American Association of Endodontists. Endodontic Diagnosis and CBCT Imaging.

q.q: What is the narrowest part of the root canal?
q.e: The apical constriction (minor diameter) is the narrowest part of the canal, usually 0.5–1 mm short of the foramen. It is the ideal end point for preparation and obturation.
q.c: Confirmed: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 gives the same answer (S01-Q224)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S01-Q224 cites: Berman LH, Hargreaves KM, eds. Cohen’s Pathways of the Pulp. 12th ed. Apical anatomy and working length.
q.n: The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.q: A patient had trauma 3 days ago (see photo). What is the treatment?
q.e: The photo shows a complicated crown fracture with a small pulp exposure. After a delay of days, a partial (Cvek) pulpotomy removes the superficially inflamed pulp and has a better prognosis than direct pulp capping, which is reserved for very recent, tiny exposures.
q.c: Consistent with a related Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 question (S01-Q166)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S01-Q166 cites: American Association of Endodontists. Recommended Guidelines for the Treatment of Traumatic Dental Injuries. 2026. Complicated crown-fracture section.
q.n: The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.q: An asymptomatic dens evaginatus is found (see photo). What is the treatment?
o: Grinding (careful, gradual reduction with dentin protection)
q.e: The tubercle usually contains a pulp horn and fractures or wears, which can expose the pulp. Prevention is gradual grinding with protection of the exposed dentin, or reinforcing it with sealant or composite. Root canal treatment is only for pulp disease.
q.c: Consistent with the October 2026 bank (OCT10-37, OCT14-102)
q.r: Where to read more: Berman LH, Hargreaves KM, eds. Cohen's Pathways of the Pulp. Dens evaginatus.
q.n: The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.q: What type of bone loss is shown in this radiograph?
q.e: The crest is level across the incisors with no angular defects, so the loss is horizontal. It reaches about half the root length or more, which counts as severe.
q.c: Answer judged from the image; Not covered in Rafi' Al-Maqam 16

q.q: A child needs two extractions and has a history of an unpleasant dental visit. What is the management?
q.e: A cooperative but anxious child having a short procedure is a classic indication for nitrous oxide–oxygen inhalation sedation. General anaesthesia is for children who can't cooperate or need extensive treatment.

q.q: What working angle should the curette face make with the tooth during scaling?
q.e: The working angulation is 45–90° (ideally about 70–80°). At 0° the blade is inserted under the gingiva, and above 90° it burnishes calculus and traumatises the soft tissue.
q.c: Confirmed: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 gives the same answer (S03-Q57)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S03-Q57 cites: Nield-Gehrig JS. Fundamentals of Periodontal Instrumentation. Curette angulation.
q.n: The recall gave 45–90 and 90–110; the other options were written in. The recall gave the options but no answer; the answer here was worked out from the references.

q.e: An EEG records the brain's electrical activity and shows epileptiform discharges.

q.q: A canine space infection (shown with a photo in the exam) most commonly arises from which tooth?
q.e: The long maxillary canine root ends above the levator anguli oris, so infection spreads into the canine space. This swells the upper lip and cheek and obliterates the nasolabial fold.
q.c: Consistent with a related Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 question (S10-Q111-C)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S10-Q111-C cites: Hupp JR, Ellis E, Tucker MR. Contemporary Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery. 7th ed. Maxillary odontogenic spaces.
